title: The four Sunan
hook: Abu Dawud, Tirmidhi, Nasa'i, Ibn Majah complete the six books

segments.voice: Yesterday: Sahih Muslim, where each hadith's chains sit side by side, and the two Sahihs as a pair.

Smiling in your brother's face is charity. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ said that, in a report from a book we haven't opened yet: the collection of al-Tirmidhi. The two Sahihs aren't the whole shelf. Beside them stand four more books, and together the six make up a set known as the six books: al-Bukhari, Muslim, and four collections with a plainer name. Today, the four Sunan.
screen: `A SMILE IS CHARITY.` → `ANOTHER BOOK.` → `FOUR MORE BOOKS.`

segments.voice: First, the word. Sunan is the plural of sunnah: ways, practices. These books are laid out like a handbook of daily life. Purity, prayer, charity, fasting, trade, marriage, food. Want to know what the Prophet did about something practical? Open a Sunan to that chapter and start reading. Second, the names. Four compilers, each known by a short name: Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i, and Ibn Majah. Say them like a roll call. Each book has its own habits. Al-Tirmidhi we met a week ago, stepping out after a report to give his verdict on it. He often also names which scholars acted on it. Third, the honest part. Sunan doesn't mean sahih. These books hold reports graded sound, reports graded good, and some graded weak, and the compilers often say so themselves. That's why this path spent days on grading before it reached the books. A hadith's book tells you where it's kept. Its grade tells you how firm it is. You want both. Fourth, the set. Al-Bukhari and Muslim, plus these four, are called the six books, al-kutub al-sitta. Scholars didn't all agree on who belongs in the sixth seat; some placed Malik's Muwatta there instead of Ibn Majah, and tomorrow we meet Malik himself. Next time you see a hadith cited with a book name and a number, you may recognize the name.
screen: `SUNAN: WAYS, PRACTICES.` · `A ROLL CALL OF FOUR NAMES.` · `SUNAN DOESN'T MEAN SAHIH.` · `THE SIXTH SEAT WAS ARGUED OVER.`

segments.voice: Count the six on your fingers, one name for each breath: on one hand, al-Bukhari and Muslim, the two Sahihs; on the other, Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i and Ibn Majah. Say them once more without looking at your hands. Then let the names rest, and keep one line from al-Tirmidhi's book: a smile in your brother's face is charity.
The four Sunan. Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i and Ibn Majah: books of the Prophet's ways, arranged by the topics of daily life. Today's word.
Your line: the six books. A book tells you where a hadith lives; a grade, how firm it is. Tomorrow: Malik and Ahmad.

howItsDone: Students of hadith learn the six books by name, and when a hadith is cited from one of the Sunan, a careful teacher checks its grade as well as its source.

notes: Tirmidhi 1956 (your smile in the face of your brother is charity): confirm number and grade; the hook says it is not in the two Sahihs. Confirm.
Al-Tirmidhi's habit of grading after a hadith and noting which scholars acted on it: a general description; confirm.
'The compilers often say so themselves' (e.g. Abu Dawud's letter to the people of Mecca, Tirmidhi's grades): confirm the generalization is fair for all four.
Some scholars put the Muwatta (others the Sunan of al-Darimi) in the sixth place instead of Ibn Majah: only the Muwatta is named here; confirm.
Al-Tirmidhi's book is usually called Jami' rather than Sunan, though it is counted among the four Sunan; the lesson keeps the outline's grouping. A Keeper may want this said.
'Known by a family name or a town': a broad description of the four names; confirm.
